newsitem.title: UK: Toyota warning echoes multinational worries.
newsitem.headline: Toyota warning echoes multinational worries.

text.p: Toyota's warning that it will have to review future investments in Britain due to a question mark over sterling's future role in a European common currency struck a chord among other leaders of international manufacturers here.
Many industrialists have been part of a slow, subtle campaign to alert British politicians to the risks of commercial complications if the pound remains a separate European currency.
Foreign companies invested an estimated 18 billion pounds ($29.2 billion) in Britain in 1995.
But by saying he feared a free-standing sterling may lessen Britain's future appeal, the Japanese carmaker's president stuck his neck out further than most of his multinational peers.

Hiroshi Okuda, a rising star in Japanese corporate life with a reputation as a straight-talker, echoed similar fears voiced by the chairman of German auto gaint BMW AG and the British head of German electronic engineer Siemens AG.
But with an imminent British election, the timing of his statement on a politically-unwelcome subject stunned several other corporate leaders.
"The currency issue does have a bearing -- I think that's inevitable for any company operating on a pan-European basis," a British director at another major global car maker told Reuters.

But like others contacted on Thursday, he declined to make formal comment, citing political sensitivities'. All were also keen to stress currency was just one of a wider list of risks encountered in making cross-border business decisions.

All of the large auto manufacturers in Britain are now internationally-based, with the twin U.S. majors General Motors Corp (via Vauxhall and Bedford) and Ford Motor Company leading the market, closely followed by BMW unit Rover.
Japan's Nissan Motor Co Ltd and Honda Motor Co Ltd join Toyota Motor Corp with car plants in England, while France's Peugeot SA also retains assembly activities here. Ford also owns Jaguar Cars.
Other manufacturers making commercial vehicles include Italy's Fiat SpA and AB Volvo of Sweden.

So, unsurprisingly, the car industry is a national business heavyweight and 1996 saw the latest round of "intervention" by the British government as it offered support amounting to tens of millions of pounds to BMW and Ford to expand production.

Nevertheless, BMW chairman Wolfgang Rietzle was not afraid to tell fellow businessmen at a London conference last autumn that he believed Britain would be "far less appealing" to inward investors if it stayed out of the currency pact.
An executive at another prominent German firm, Siemens AG, made his latest sortie in this war of attrition two weeks ago.

Siemens plc chief executive Jurgen Gehrels told reporters he did not think the group would have begun a 1.1 billion pound semiconductor plant in 1995 if it had felt Britain would stay out of a common currency for ever.
"If it had been clear that Britain would be out of a single currency at the time we invested in North Tyneside then that decision would have gone another way," he was quoted as saying.
Among other companies and sectors the feeling is more that this is a problem that does not need to be confronted yet.

While many of the South Korean electronics manufacturers who have recently arrived on Britain's high-technology landscape with new factories studied the currency risk in detail they have opted for the long view, a source at one company told Reuters.
"Back home the companies are taking a long-range view of Britain. They feel sterling will not join a common currency in 1999 but at some time later, so they do not worry yet," he said.
